claims.text: Classical molecular dynamics with EAM potentials calibrated for FeCuCrCoNi can be used to study the thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles.
The thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles is significantly size-dependent.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower effective melting or transition temperatures than larger particles.
The initial materials are synthesized FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles with nanoscale microstructures typical of experimental synthesis.
The proposed simulation applies a temperature ramp from 300 K to 1500 K in 50 K increments.
Particle diameters ranging from 5 nm to 50 nm are proposed for comparison.
The nanoparticles are proposed to be simulated under isobaric-isothermal conditions.
Simulation durations are specified as up to 10 ns.
Surface diffusion and internal lattice rearrangements mediate the onset of melting or other significant structural transitions.
Increasing thermal energy enhances atomic mobility and diffusion.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller particles causes enhanced disorder or melting at lower temperatures.
Decreasing particle size lowers the critical temperature for melting or structural disordering.
No significant structural transition is expected at the 300 K baseline.
A 10 ns simulation timescale may not capture long-term thermal diffusion processes.
The results depend on the accuracy of the EAM potential calibration for the multielement alloy.
Quantum effects may introduce uncertainty at very small particle sizes.
Transition temperatures can be identified using structural order parameters, diffusion coefficients, and surface-atom mobility.
The hypothesis is falsified if smaller particles do not consistently exhibit lower transition temperatures than larger particles.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify simulation durations of up to 10 ns, whereas the falsification design requires at least 10 ns at every temperature step; these timing specifications are inconsistent unless the former is intended as a per-step duration.
